title: Discrete Mathematics
tagline: Counting, recurrences, generating functions and graph theory
summary: Discrete mathematics deals with finite and countable structures: arrangements, networks and recursive processes. This course covers counting techniques, recurrence relations and generating functions, and graph theory from basic definitions to algorithms, colouring and planarity.
overview: Discrete mathematics studies objects that come in separate, countable pieces — finite sets, integers, arrangements, networks — rather than the continuously varying quantities of calculus. Its questions are often easy to state and surprisingly deep. In how many ways can a committee be chosen? How many moves does the Tower of Hanoi need? Can every map be coloured with four colours? What is the shortest route through a road network? Answering them takes a toolkit of counting principles, recursive thinking and graph theory that is also the mathematical backbone of computer science.

The course has two halves. Chapters 1–4 are about counting: the sum and product rules, permutations, combinations and the binomial theorem; the pigeonhole principle and inclusion–exclusion; recurrence relations and how to solve them; and generating functions, which turn sequences into power series and counting problems into algebra. Chapters 5–7 are graph theory: the vocabulary of vertices, edges, paths and trees; algorithms for searching graphs, finding shortest paths and minimum spanning trees, and Euler and Hamilton tours; and finally planarity, colouring and matchings.

We assume the logic, sets, functions and induction of the Foundations course. Counting arguments are easy to get subtly wrong — by counting something twice or overlooking a case — so much of learning the subject is learning to check: test every formula on small cases by hand, look for a bijective explanation, and prove general claims by induction. Graph theory rewards drawing pictures, but a picture is never a proof, and the theorems here are proved with the same care as in analysis.
outcomes: Count arrangements and selections with the sum and product rules, permutations, combinations and the binomial theorem, and prove identities by double counting.
Apply the pigeonhole principle and inclusion–exclusion, and count derangements and distributions with stars and bars.
Model problems with recurrence relations and solve linear recurrences with constant coefficients.
Use ordinary generating functions to solve recurrences and counting problems, including problems about integer partitions.
Use the language of graphs — degree, path, connectivity, isomorphism, tree — and prove the handshake lemma and the basic characterisations of trees.
Run and justify breadth- and depth-first search, Dijkstra's shortest-path algorithm and the minimum spanning tree algorithms of Prim and Kruskal.
Decide when a graph has an Euler circuit, and explain why finding Hamilton cycles is believed to be much harder.
Apply Euler's formula to planar graphs, bound chromatic numbers, and use Hall's theorem to decide when a matching exists.

history.title: Fibonacci's rabbits
history.detail: Leonardo of Pisa's *Liber Abaci* poses the rabbit-breeding problem whose answer is the Fibonacci sequence, the most famous recurrence relation.

history.title: Pascal's arithmetic triangle
history.detail: Blaise Pascal writes his *Traité du triangle arithmétique* (published in 1665), proving properties of binomial coefficients by an early form of induction. The triangle itself was known centuries earlier in India, Persia and China.

history.title: The bridges of Königsberg
history.detail: Leonhard Euler shows that no walk crosses each of Königsberg's seven bridges exactly once, the first theorem of graph theory.

history.title: Generating functions for partitions
history.detail: In his *Introductio in analysin infinitorum* Euler counts partitions of integers with infinite products, and proves that partitions into distinct parts and into odd parts are equinumerous.

history.title: The four colour problem
history.detail: Francis Guthrie notices that four colours suffice for a map of the counties of England and asks whether this is always true; the question reaches Augustus De Morgan through his brother Frederick.

history.title: Hamilton's icosian game
history.detail: William Rowan Hamilton presents a puzzle asking for a round trip through the 20 vertices of a dodecahedron, the origin of the term Hamilton cycle.

history.title: Kuratowski's theorem
history.detail: Kazimierz Kuratowski proves that a graph is planar unless it contains a subdivision of $K_5$ or $K_{3,3}$.

history.title: Hall's marriage theorem
history.detail: Philip Hall gives the condition for a family of sets to have distinct representatives, the basic theorem on matchings in bipartite graphs.

history.title: Shortest paths and spanning trees
history.detail: Edsger Dijkstra publishes his shortest-path algorithm, following the minimum spanning tree algorithms of Joseph Kruskal (1956) and Robert Prim (1957); Otakar Borůvka had studied spanning trees as early as 1926.

history.title: The four colour theorem
history.detail: Kenneth Appel and Wolfgang Haken prove that every planar map can be four-coloured, using a computer to check almost two thousand configurations.
